paras: The Thebes lynching and attack on Black construction camps took place on April 26, 1903, near Santa Fe and Thebes in Alexander County, Illinois, when a mob of white farmers took a Black youth of about seventeen from officers and hanged him. The mob then shot into and burned a camp of Black bridge workers. Indictments and trials followed in Cairo without a reported conviction.

Several hundred Black men building a new Mississippi River bridge lived in tents near Santa Fe, and several hundred more working on the St. Louis Valley Railroad lived at Coles Camp, north of Thebes. According to the wire report, a young Black man accosted the ten-year-old daughter of farmer Branson Davis and fled when she screamed; he was accused of attempting to assault her.

Officers caught the youth, but a mob of farmers met them on the road to Santa Fe and seized him after what the dispatch called a "scrimmage." The dispatch stated that he confessed before he was hanged from an oak tree and his body riddled with bullets, while officers tried in vain to disperse the mob.

The mob next rushed the bridge workers' tents. In the wire version the workers fired first, many were shot down, and no whites were hurt; the workers fled, and the mob burned the tents. State's Attorney Wilson later said the white men also broke open trunks and stole clothing and shoes. At midnight whites raided Coles Camp and drove its workers away, and men who tried to return the next morning were fired on. No lives were known lost, though more Black men were hurt than first supposed.

In May a Cairo grand jury returned one indictment for murder and three for rioting, and Sheriff Roche arrested John Hickson of Thebes, said to have bound the youth's hands. Harry Lacelle, Harry Petit and Ed Irish were tried in county court in July, with no verdict found, and the county paid contractor George A. Welsh $521.82 for his destroyed camp. In December five Thebes men charged with lynching "William Johnson (colored)," the only name given for the victim, were discharged for insufficient evidence by J. E. Jackson, a Black justice of the peace. Henry Metcalf and Fred Kenner were held on murder charges in January 1904.

Hickson, later called Napoleon, was tried in October 1903 before a jury "composed almost wholly of negroes" that could not agree. Unable to raise $2,000 bail, he escaped jail in April 1904, and in May the state dropped the case because its witnesses could not be had. In June a Springfield report said Thebes Black residents had written three times to the governor seeking help to serve warrants.

The Associated Press dispatch ran on front pages nationwide under heads such as "GENERAL ATTACK ON NEGROES," calling the youth "the assailant" and reporting his confession as fact. Follow-ups were headed "A RACE WAR" and "Negroes Wounded in a Riot," and a Richmond Times-Dispatch editorial used the lynching for "the usual crime" to argue that trouble followed Black people into the North. Later Cairo, Paducah and St. Louis coverage treated it as court news.

Three Black weeklies took it up on May 2. The Baltimore Afro-American reran the wire story with "colored" for "negro" under the headline "The Whites Shoot Many Blacks." The Chicago Broad Ax called the victim a "nameless Negro," stressed that the mob of "white gentlemen" fired on hundreds of workers with no connection to the accused, and said Illinois was "joining hands with S. C." The Indianapolis Freeman answered that "the laws can cope with all such offenses." Black lynching tallies listed an "Unknown Negro" at Thebes on April 26; no Black-press report of the trials was found.

The June Springfield report dated the camp shooting March 26 and counted one killed and one injured, whereas reports written at the time give April 26 and no known deaths in the camps. The wire said the workers fired first, while the Broad Ax said the mob opened fire on them. Reports placed the lynching variously in the afternoon and at night.

reader.title: Thebes lynching and attack on Black construction camps
bases: A mob took an accused Black youth from officers and hanged and shot him, then attacked and burned a camp of Black workers and drove others from a second camp (A1, A2, A4); the camp attacks are part of the same episode, not a separate community attack.

The lynching and the camp attack are reported by the April wire, separate follow-up dispatches, Cairo court reports and three Black papers (A1, A4, A5, A7, A9, A11); the record's version, a March 26 shooting into a railroad camp with one killed, appears only in a single secondhand June summary (A12).

accounts.gist: The youth accosted the Davis girl, was caught by officers, taken by farmers, confessed and was hanged and shot; the camp workers fired first as the mob approached, and many were shot while no whites were hurt.

accounts.label: Black residents' complaint (via Springfield report)
accounts.gist: White men shot into a railroad camp, killing one and injuring another; the workers were driven off and their property taken; they could identify the shooters but could not get warrants served.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'GENERAL ATTACK ON NEGROES' and 'Tents Burned and Many Laborers Are Shot' over a wire story that called the victim 'the assailant' and stated his confession as fact.
Follow-ups headed 'A RACE WAR' and 'Negroes Wounded in a Riot' reported white threats and the expulsion of workers without comment.
A Richmond editorial used the case, a lynching for 'the usual crime', to argue that trouble follows wherever Black people gather in the North.

Cairo, Paducah and St. Louis papers reported the grand jury, trials and dismissals as court news under heads like 'LYNCHERS ON TRIAL' and 'THEBES LYNCHERS'; one Cairo item complained that Hickson's bail was excessive.
The Broad Ax mocked the 'white gentlemen' of the mob and said Illinois was 'joining hands with S. C.'; the Freeman said the laws could cope with such offenses.
The Afro-American ran the wire story under 'THE WHITES SHOOT MANY BLACKS', with 'colored' for 'negro'; lynching lists recorded an 'Unknown Negro' at Thebes on April 26.

conflicts.note: Every contemporaneous dispatch and the Black-press lists give April 26; the March date appears only in a June summary written two months later and is likely an error for the same episode.
The first dispatch says 'this afternoon'; the next day's dispatch and the Broad Ax say night.
